strands.title: Feudalism, labour forms and capitalist development
strands.focus: Dobb gives priority to production relations while allowing trade to interact with conflict. Sweezy questions definition and regional transfer; Takahashi develops labour-form analysis and challenges limited coverage. These are distinct positions.
strands.works: Studies (1946); Sweezy–Dobb exchange (1950); Takahashi contribution (1952)

strands.title: Revolution, religion and radical alternatives
strands.focus: Hill’s 1955 revision call and 1972 radical inquiry have different emphases. Dobb’s resource, Hilton’s draft advice and Barg’s comparative work reveal concrete exchanges; belief and unrealized alternatives belong within social explanation.
strands.works: Hill (1955 preface; 1972; 1986 review)

strands.title: Class formation, labour and popular politics
strands.focus: The Thompsons and Hobsbawm investigate different objects. Experience, organization, families and political language cannot be collapsed into one class model.

strands.title: Collective research, tutoring and public history

strands.title: Crowds, markets and customary legitimacy
strands.focus: Rudé supplies an explicit resource for Thompson’s inquiry into how people justify and organize market protest. Material deprivation matters, but it does not by itself explain collective action.
strands.works: The Crowd in History (1964); “The Moral Economy of the English Crowd” (1971)

strands.title: Time, labour and industrial discipline
strands.focus: Thompson combines historical and anthropological resources to examine work rhythms, wages, education and coercion. Task and clock time overlap; transformation is uneven.
strands.works: “Time, Work-Discipline, and Industrial Capitalism” (1967)

strands.title: Empire and international exchanges
strands.focus: Kiernan’s diplomacy and James’s Caribbean revolution widen the British focus in different ways. Hobsbawm recalls reading James despite political divisions; James retains an independent intellectual project.
strands.works: British Diplomacy in China, 1880 to 1885 (1939); The Black Jacobins (1938; revised 1963)

strands.title: Gender, family and the making of class
strands.focus: Dorothy Thompson, Taylor and Clark pursue different combinations of class and gender inquiry. Feminist inheritance and criticism coexist, as do disagreements about cooperation and conflict.
strands.works: “Women and Nineteenth-Century Radical Politics” (1976); Eve and the New Jerusalem (1983); The Struggle for the Breeches (1995)

strands.title: Language, experience and contested class interpretation
strands.focus: Stedman Jones questions political idioms; Kirk defends a class interpretation with limited claims. Dorothy insists language already requires contextual reading. These interventions do not form one debate between two uniform camps.
strands.works: Languages of Class (1983); “In Defence of Class” (1987); Dorothy Thompson interview

strands.title: Peasant movements, belief and political aims
strands.focus: Hilton compares 1381 with continental movements while examining aims, allies and outcomes. Conflict does not mean constant open warfare; economic/social relations require political and religious analysis. Neither quick defeat nor later change settles causation.
strands.works: Bond Men Made Free (1973), selected introduction and conclusion

before.label: History Workshop movement
before.description: Develops collaborative history from below through adult education, labour movements, and historical scholarship. Its socialist and feminist projects involve worker-historians alongside academic historians. Oral testimony, women’s history, and later work on popular memory reshape its concerns.

strands.title: Adult education and collaborative history
strands.focus: Ruskin students’ research and cheaply produced pamphlets connect participation, audiences and publication.
strands.works: History Workshop pamphlets (1970–74), described by Davin; archive introduction

strands.title: Socialist feminist history
strands.focus: Feminist organizing changes subjects and internal priorities; the 1969 dispute and 1970 Ruskin conference expose negotiation.
strands.works: Rowbotham, Hidden from History (1973); Workshop 4 archive account

strands.title: Contested linguistic reorientation
strands.focus: Stedman Jones questions class’s assumed political meaning; this is one intervention within a heterogeneous movement.
strands.works: Languages of Class (1983), introduction opening

strands.title: Oral history in publication and teaching
strands.focus: The 1976 journal article supplies an early venue; Taylor’s recollection documents Davin teaching oral history in 1998.
strands.works: Samuel (1976); Davin’s teaching, recalled by Becky Taylor (2025)

strands.title: Gender and the domestic history of empire
strands.focus: Davin’s study of motherhood connects metropolitan gender questions to imperial politics.
strands.works: “Imperialism and Motherhood” (1978), discussed retrospectively by its author

strands.title: Feminist history and psychoanalytic questions
strands.focus: Sexual difference and subjectivity open questions about historical actors and the historian’s interpretation.
strands.works: Becoming a Woman (1994)

strands.title: Popular historical practices
strands.focus: Samuel examines historical knowledge made through everyday cultural activity.
strands.works: Theatres of Memory (1994)

strands.title: Spatial history and contested places
strands.focus: Driver and Samuel’s editorial accompanies Massey’s intervention on changing place identities and histories.
strands.works: History Workshop Journal 39 (1995), spatial-history section

strands.title: Collaborative place history
strands.focus: The 1995 spatial-history section includes Rita and Jackie Huggins with Jane M. Jacobs. Verified coauthorship and the public finding aid document collaboration; detailed article interpretation remains limited by access.
strands.works: Kooramindanjie: Place and the Postcolonial (1995)

strands.title: Oral and documentary evidence in interaction
strands.focus: Samuel treats local history as an inquiry shaped by available sources and questions. Oral evidence can expose archival omissions but has its own silences and retrospective distortions.
strands.works: Local History and Oral History (1976), selected reprint passages

strands.title: Empire, class and definitions of motherhood
strands.focus: Davin examines how imperial concerns and professional authority made mothers responsible for population health. Her account differentiates pressures on women across class positions.
strands.works: Imperialism and Motherhood (1978), opening and research credits

strands.title: Worker history and union authority
strands.focus: Douglass examines tensions between miners, employers and union officials, connecting historical disputes with his own experience of workplace representation.
strands.works: Pit Life in Co. Durham (1972), attributed excerpt

strands.title: Chartist language and class explanations
strands.focus: Stedman Jones questions explanations that derive political mobilization directly from hardship. Kirk accepts attention to language but disputes its relative autonomy and the marginalization of anti-capitalist ideas.
strands.works: Rethinking Chartism (1983); In Defence of Class (1987), selected passages

after.scope_note: Adult education, socialist research, feminist criticism, and linguistic debates interact; no single turn describes the whole movement. The Ruskin workshops, later itinerant meetings and journal are related institutions with distinct histories. Retrospective participant accounts supply evidence about earlier practice without extending this map beyond 2000.

after.relationship: Stedman Jones’s account of class idioms offers a linguistic reorientation within British social-history debates
after.evidence_note: Stedman Jones’s work is not a unified linguistic turn of the whole Workshop movement. The primary introduction opening supplies the specific question about class’s political meaning. The comparison does not establish a uniform Workshop linguistic turn. Selected Chartism passages and Kirk’s criticism now specify the disagreement. Both resist economic reductionism; they differ over political language’s autonomy. This paired reading does not establish a reciprocal published reply.

outcomes.finding: An attributed original pamphlet excerpt supplies Douglass’s own argument; paired Chartism passages and Kirk’s criticism specify agreement and disagreement beyond earlier opening notes. Original-scan and reciprocal-reply limits remain explicit.
outcomes.research_limit: Douglass: complete attributed “The leadership and the rank and file” excerpt read in a later online reproduction; no original scan collation, page interval or complete pamphlet reading. Embedded Webbs quotation and later criticism of Douglass are separate textual layers. Official Douglass and Moyo uploads yielded metadata without readable original bodies; Moyo’s position is not inferred. Stedman Jones: 90–98 and 173–178 plus acknowledgments read in public transcription; intervening chapter incomplete, no original-printing or 1982 essay collation. Kirk: 6–7, 14–17 and complete conclusion 46–47 read, supplementing prior opening/notes; most middle body unread. Paired intervention and contemporary criticism, not a verified reciprocal reply. No universal worker voice or uniform Workshop doctrine inferred.
